The National Population Council (CONAPO) is an institution under the Ministry of Interior in charge of the analysis and research of population dynamics. Greater Mexico City is the largest metropolitan area in Mexico and the area with the highest population density. ![](image)INEGI's headquarters.
The **National Institute of Statistics and Geography** (**INEGI** from its former name in Template:Lang-es) is an autonomous agency of the Mexican Government dedicated to coordinate the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information of the country.[1] It was created on January 25, 1983, by presidential decree of Miguel de la Madrid.


</fragment>
<fragment>

It is the institution responsible for conducting the Censo General de Población y Vivienda every ten years; as well as the economic census every five years and the agricultural, livestock and forestry census of the country. The job of gathering statistical information of the Institute includes the monthly gross domestic product, consumer trust surveys and proportion of commercial samples; employment and occupation statistics, domestic and couple violence; as well as many other jobs that are the basis of studies and projections to other governmental institutions.


The Institute headquarters are in the city of Aguascalientes in central Mexico.

With the enactment of the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information Law, (LSNIEG by its name in Spanish, *Ley del Sistema Nacional de Información Estadística y Geográfica*) on April 16, 2008, INEGI changed its legal personality, acquiring technical and management autonomy. Its new denomination is National Institute of Statistic and Geography (INEGI by its name in Spanish, Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía), but it preserves the acronym of its former name (INEGI).


INEGI's main objective is to achieve that the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information (SNIEG, by its name in Spanish), bring to the society and to the government, quality information, pertinent, truthful and relevant, to contribute to the national development, under accessibility, transparency, objectivity and independence principles.

根据维基百科上的官方 2020 年人口普查数据，由 INEGI（国家统计和地理研究所）收集的墨西哥城区人口信息如下：

## **城区中心区的人口（ Ciudad de México 行政区）**
- **2020 年：9,209,944**
- **2010 年：8,851,080**
- **增长：+4.1%**

## **大墨西哥城区的人口**
- **2020 年：总人口：21,804,515**
  - 墨西哥城中心区：9,209,944
  - 大都市区其他部分：12,594,571
- 这包括大墨西哥山谷都市圈，该都市圈包含墨西哥城区及附近各州的部分区域

## **人口密度**
- **墨西哥城中心区：** 每平方公里 6,163.4 人
- **大都市区：** 拉丁美洲人口密度最高

## **数据来源**
这些都是来自 INEGI 的官方数据，墨西哥每十年进行一次人口普查。搜索中提到 2005 年至 2050 年间的大墨西哥山谷都市圈（按 2005 年定义）有数据预测。

墨西哥城区仍然是西半球人口最多的大都市区，也是世界上最主要的城区之一。

Greater Mexico City's main industries are now related to trade, financial services, insurance companies, telecommunications, informatics and transportation.[16] In spite of the recent shifts in economic production and the decentralization of the economic activity promoted by the government, Greater Mexico City's share of total economic activity in the country is still high, though decreasing. Mexico City proper alone produces $170 billion or 17% of the nation's Gross Domestic Product, larger than any of the states.[17]



## Demographics

[edit]

![](image)Growth of the urban area from 1900 to 2000
Greater Mexico City is the largest metropolitan area in Mexico and the area with the highest population density. According to the 2020 Population Census, 21,804,515 persons lived in this metropolitan area, of which 9,209,944 live in Mexico City proper.[5] Approximately 72% (12.2 million) of the State of México's population live in municipalities that are part of Greater Mexico City's conurbation.

8. **^** "Delimitation of the Metropolitan Areas in Mexico" (PDF) (in Spanish). CONAPO. Retrieved 2020-12-30.

<fragment>

Greater Mexico City was the fastest-growing metropolitan area in the country until the late 1980s. Since then, and through a policy of decentralization in order to reduce the environmental pollutants of the growing conurbation, the annual rate of growth of the agglomeration has decreased, and it is among the lowest of all metropolitan areas in Mexico. The net migration rate of Mexico City proper from 1995 to 2000, however, was negative,[18] which implies that residents are moving to the outer suburbs of the metropolitan area, or to other states of Mexico. In addition, some inner-city suburbs in Mexico City are losing population to outer city suburbs, indicating a continual expansion of Greater Mexico City.



### Human development index

[edit]

The Mexico City boroughs are among the subdivisions with the highest human development in Mexico. Benito Juárez has the highest index (0.944), similar to Australia or Netherlands, while 4 other boroughs are in the national Top 10.[19]

<document>
<title>Demographics of Mexico</title>
<fragment>

Demographic censuses are performed by the Instituto Nacional de Estadística, Geografía e Informatica. The National Population Council (CONAPO) is an institution under the Ministry of Interior in charge of the analysis and research of population dynamics. The National Commission for the Development of Indigenous Peoples (CDI), also undertakes research and analysis of the sociodemographic and linguistic indicators of the indigenous peoples.




## Demographic dynamics

[edit]

See also: Mexicans

The Mexican government projects[15] that the Mexican population will grow to about 123 million by 2042 and then start declining slowly. Assumptions underlying this projection include fertility stabilizing at 1.85 children per woman and continued high net emigration (slowly decreasing from 583,000 in 2005 to 393,000 in 2050).


The states and Mexico City that make up the Mexican federation are collectively called "federal entities". The five most populous federal entities in 2005 were the State of Mexico (14.4 million), Mexico City (8.7 million), Veracruz (7.1 million), Jalisco (6.7 million) and Puebla (5.4 million), which collectively contain 40.7% of the national population. Mexico City, being coextensive with the Mexico City, is the most populous city in the country, while Greater Mexico City, that includes the adjacent municipalities that comprise a metropolitan area, is estimated to be the second most populous in the world (after Tokyo), according to the UN Urbanization Report.


</fragment>

![](image)INEGI's headquarters.
The **National Institute of Statistics and Geography** (**INEGI** from its former name in Template:Lang-es) is an autonomous agency of the Mexican Government dedicated to coordinate the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information of the country.[1] It was created on January 25, 1983, by presidential decree of Miguel de la Madrid.


</fragment>
<fragment>

It is the institution responsible for conducting the Censo General de Población y Vivienda every ten years; as well as the economic census every five years and the agricultural, livestock and forestry census of the country. The job of gathering statistical information of the Institute includes the monthly gross domestic product, consumer trust surveys and proportion of commercial samples; employment and occupation statistics, domestic and couple violence; as well as many other jobs that are the basis of studies and projections to other governmental institutions.


The Institute headquarters are in the city of Aguascalientes in central Mexico.

With the enactment of the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information Law, (LSNIEG by its name in Spanish, *Ley del Sistema Nacional de Información Estadística y Geográfica*) on April 16, 2008, INEGI changed its legal personality, acquiring technical and management autonomy. Its new denomination is National Institute of Statistic and Geography (INEGI by its name in Spanish, Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía), but it preserves the acronym of its former name (INEGI).


INEGI's main objective is to achieve that the National System of Statistical and Geographical Information (SNIEG, by its name in Spanish), bring to the society and to the government, quality information, pertinent, truthful and relevant, to contribute to the national development, under accessibility, transparency, objectivity and independence principles.

<document>
<title>Demographics of Mexico</title>
<fragment>

Demographic censuses are performed by the Instituto Nacional de Estadística, Geografía e Informatica. The National Population Council (CONAPO) is an institution under the Ministry of Interior in charge of the analysis and research of population dynamics. The National Commission for the Development of Indigenous Peoples (CDI), also undertakes research and analysis of the sociodemographic and linguistic indicators of the indigenous peoples.

## **Available Official Data:**

**Mexico City Proper (Administrative City Limits):**
- **2020 Census**: 9,209,944 inhabitants
- **2020 Land Area**: 1,495 square kilometers (577 sq mi)
- **2020 Population Density**: ~6,163 people per km²

**Greater Mexico City Metropolitan Area:**
- **2020 Definition**: 21,804,515 inhabitants 
- **2019 Estimate**: 21,671,908 inhabitants
- Makes it the 6th-largest metropolitan area in the world

## **Limitations in Available Data:**

❌ **Missing from Available Sources:**
- 2021-2023 population estimates
- Age and gender breakdowns
- Religious affiliation data
- Economic status distribution

## **Why This Data Isn't Available Through Wikipedia:**

The detailed 2021-2023 demographic breakdowns you're seeking are typically published through:
1. **INEGI's** annual population bulletins and demographic reports
2. **CONAPO's** population projection reports
3. **Mexican government statistical databases**

These official inter-annual estimates and demographic breakdowns are not always immediately incorporated into Wikipedia articles, as they require access to the original government statistical publications.

## **Recommendations for Finding This Data:**

To obtain the specific 2021-2023 population estimates with age/gender breakdowns, you would need to access:

1. **INEGI website** (inegi.org.mx) - Look for annual population estimates
2. **CONAPO website** (conapo.gob.mx) - Population projection reports  
3. **Mexico City government statistics portal** - Local demographic updates
4. **Mexico's national data portal** (datos.gob.mx) - Official government statistics

The most recent official comprehensive data available through accessible sources remains the 2020 Census figures.

São Paulo's population has grown rapidly. By 1960 it had surpassed that of Rio de Janeiro, making it Brazil's most populous city. By this time, the urbanized area of São Paulo had extended beyond the boundaries of the municipality proper into neighboring municipalities, making it a metropolitan area with a population of 4.6 million. Population growth has continued since 1960, although the rate of growth has slowed.[85]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 2013, São Paulo was the most populous city in Brazil and in South America.[86] According to the 2010 IBGE Census, there were 11,244,369 people residing in the city of São Paulo.[87] Portuguese remains the most widely spoken language and São Paulo is the largest city in the Portuguese speaking world.[88]


In 2010, the city had 2,146,077 opposite-sex couples and 7,532 same-sex couples. The population of São Paulo was 52.6% female and 47.4% male.[89] The census found 6,824,668 White people (60.6%), 3,433,218 Pardo (multiracial) people (30.5%), 736,083 Black people (6.5%), 246,244 Asian people (2.2%) and 21,318 Amerindian people (0.2%).[89]

### Distribution

[edit]




</fragment>
<fragment>
![A map of Brazil, with purple circles denoting areas of high population in the year 2000. A large majority of the circles line Brazil's eastern coast.](image)Population distribution in Brazil.
Brazil has a high level of urbanization with 87.8%[1] of the population residing in urban and metropolitan areas. The criteria used by the IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)[2] in determining whether households are urban or rural, however, are based on political divisions, not on the developed environment.


Nowadays, the country has 5,570 cities, with 5,568 municipalities plus the capital and the Island of Fernando de Noronha.[3]


With two exceptions, the state capitals are all the largest cities in their respective states: Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina is its second-largest city after Joinville, while Vitória is only the fourth-largest city in Espírito Santo, although it is located in that state's largest metropolitan area.

The **2022 Brazilian Census** was the thirteenth national population census in Brazilian history, and took place on August 1, 2022. It was intended to take place in 2020, but postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and budgetary issues.



## Delays

[edit]

Originally, the census, being carried out decennially, was supposed to take place in mid-2020. However, due to the current COVID-19 pandemic, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics changed the date to 2021.[1]


However, in early 2021, the budget of census was cut from around 2 billion reais to only 240 million, only 12% of the original value.[2] The census was pushed again, with Brazil's Supreme Court ruling that the government had to perform the census in 2022.[3]


While the original reference date was June 1, 2022, the IBGE changed the date to August 1, 2022, due to the change in the company that would hire the workers.[4]

Brazil's population, as recorded by the 2010 census, was of 190,755,799 inhabitants[6] (22.40 inhabitants per square kilometer), with 84.36% of the population defined as urban. The population is heavily concentrated in the Southeast (80.4 million) and Northeast (53.1 million).



### Distribution

[edit]




</fragment>
<fragment>
![A map of Brazil, with purple circles denoting areas of high population in the year 2000. A large majority of the circles line Brazil's eastern coast.](image)Population distribution in Brazil.
Brazil has a high level of urbanization with 87.8%[1] of the population residing in urban and metropolitan areas. The criteria used by the IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)[2] in determining whether households are urban or rural, however, are based on political divisions, not on the developed environment.


Nowadays, the country has 5,570 cities, with 5,568 municipalities plus the capital and the Island of Fernando de Noronha.[3]


With two exceptions, the state capitals are all the largest cities in their respective states: Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina is its second-largest city after Joinville, while Vitória is only the fourth-largest city in Espírito Santo, although it is located in that state's largest metropolitan area.

A simpler population count *(contagem de população)* is theoretically made in the interval between two censuses, starting in 1996. These aim to update the data on the number of inhabitants, of great importance to Brazil's cities, because annual grants from the Municipalities Participation Fund are determined mainly by population. The IBGE is responsible for estimating populations annually for every municipality in the country, and these population counts enhance the quality of estimates.[14]


The first population count was conducted in 1996, not only to update population data, but also to get municipality level data after the emergence and redefinition of new municipalities after the census of 1991. The most recent count was done in 2007, delayed from 2005 because of budgetary concerns,[14] and the 2016 count was completely cancelled for similar reasons.[15]



### Agricultural census

[edit]

<fragment>
The best known census is the population census (Template:Lang-pt-BR). First conducted in its modern form in 1872, it is now conducted every ten years, usually in years ending in zero. No census took place in 1880, 1910 or 1930.[10]


The census is conducted solely by the IBGE, as enshrined in law. Comprehensive demographic data is collected on the population (including age, income, sex, etc.), as well as housing stock.[11] Unlike approaches taken in other countries (e.g., the United States), the questionnaire asks respondents to self-identify by skin color,[10] phrasing the question as "Color or Race".[12]

The **2022 Brazilian Census** was the thirteenth national population census in Brazilian history, and took place on August 1, 2022. It was intended to take place in 2020, but postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and budgetary issues.



## Delays

[edit]

Originally, the census, being carried out decennially, was supposed to take place in mid-2020. However, due to the current COVID-19 pandemic, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics changed the date to 2021.[1]


However, in early 2021, the budget of census was cut from around 2 billion reais to only 240 million, only 12% of the original value.[2] The census was pushed again, with Brazil's Supreme Court ruling that the government had to perform the census in 2022.[3]


While the original reference date was June 1, 2022, the IBGE changed the date to August 1, 2022, due to the change in the company that would hire the workers.[4]

The RMSP of São Paulo is known as a financial and economic centre of Brazil, with a total population of 20,743,587 inhabitants (2022 census[4]). The ABC Region (from Santo André, São Bernardo do Campo and São Caetano do Sul) in the south of Grande São Paulo is an important location for industrial corporations, such as Volkswagen and Ford. Based on the 2022 Brazilian Census data, here's a comprehensive breakdown of the demographics of Brazil:

## **Overview**
The 2022 Brazilian Census was the thirteenth national census in Brazil's history, conducted on August 1, 2022. It recorded Brazil's total population as **203,062,512** inhabitants.

## **Geographic Distribution**

### **Most and Least Populous States:**
- **Most populous:** São Paulo State
- **Least populous:** Roraima State

### **Regional Population Concentration:**
Based on historical patterns, the population is heavily concentrated in:
- **Southeast Region:** ~80.4 million inhabitants
- **Northeast Region:** ~53.1 million inhabitants

## **Urban vs. Rural Distribution**
From 2010 census data (showing the pattern):
- **Urban population:** 84.36% 
- **Rural population:** 15.64%

## **Major Urban Centers**

### **Largest Metropolitan Areas:**

#### **São Paulo Metropolitan Area:**
- **Total population:** 20,743,587 inhabitants (2022 census)
- **Core city population:** 11,451,245 (São Paulo city)
- **Other major municipalities:**
  - Guarulhos: 1,291,784
  - São Bernardo do Campo: 810,729
  - Santo André: 748,919

#### **Other Major Metropolitan Regions:**
- **Campinas Metropolitan Region:** 3,631,528
- **Vale do Paraíba e Litoral Norte:** 2,575,879  
- **Sorocaba Metropolitan Region:** 2,108,425
- **Baixada Santista:** 1,913,033

### **Most Populous Municipalities:**
1. **São Paulo** (São Paulo)
2. **Rio de Janeiro** (Rio de Janeiro)
3. **Brasília** (Federal District)
4. **Fortaleza** (Ceará)
5. **Salvador** (Bahia)
6. **Belo Horizonte** (Minas Gerais)
7. **Manaus** (Amazonas)
8. **Curitiba** (Paraná)
9. **Recife** (Pernambuco)
10. **Goiânia** (Goiás)

## **Population Distribution by State (Cities over 100,000 inhabitants):**
- **São Paulo:** 78 cities
- **Minas Gerais:** 34 cities
- **Rio de Janeiro:** 28 cities
- **Paraná:** 22 cities
- **Rio Grande do Sul:** 19 cities
- **Bahia:** 18 cities

## **Historical Context**
The census was originally scheduled for 2020 but was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and budgetary issues. The Supreme Court ruled that the government had to perform the census in 2022, and the reference date was changed from June 1 to August 1, 2022.

## **Key Demographic Trends**
The data shows Brazil's continued urbanization, with the vast majority of the population living in urban centers, particularly in the southeastern and northeastern regions of the country. The São Paulo metropolitan area remains by far the largest urban agglomeration in Brazil and one of the largest in the world.

**Note:** While I searched for detailed racial/ethnic breakdown from the 2022 census, the specific categorical data for the 2022 census was not available in the sources accessed. Brazil traditionally uses five main racial categories in its census: White, Black (Preto), Brown/Mixed (Pardo), Asian (Amarelo), and Indigenous (Indígena), based on self-identification.

Brazil has a high level of urbanization with 87.8%[1] of the population residing in urban and metropolitan areas. The criteria used by the IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics)[2] in determining whether households are urban or rural, however, are based on political divisions, not on the developed environment.


Nowadays, the country has 5,570 cities, with 5,568 municipalities plus the capital and the Island of Fernando de Noronha.[3]


With two exceptions, the state capitals are all the largest cities in their respective states: Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina is its second-largest city after Joinville, while Vitória is only the fourth-largest city in Espírito Santo, although it is located in that state's largest metropolitan area.

The **2022 Brazilian Census** was the thirteenth national population census in Brazilian history, and took place on August 1, 2022. It was intended to take place in 2020, but postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and budgetary issues.



## Delays

[edit]

Originally, the census, being carried out decennially, was supposed to take place in mid-2020. However, due to the current COVID-19 pandemic, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics changed the date to 2021.[1]


However, in early 2021, the budget of census was cut from around 2 billion reais to only 240 million, only 12% of the original value.[2] The census was pushed again, with Brazil's Supreme Court ruling that the government had to perform the census in 2022.[3]


While the original reference date was June 1, 2022, the IBGE changed the date to August 1, 2022, due to the change in the company that would hire the workers.[4]

**New York**, often called **New York City**[b] or simply **NYC**, is the most populous city in the United States. With a census-estimated population of 8,335,897 distributed over 300.46 square miles (778.2 km2) in 2022,[4] the city is the most densely populated major city in the United States. NYC is more than twice as populous as Los Angeles, the nation's second-most populous city. New York City is at the southern tip of New York State and is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. The city comprises five boroughs, each of which is coextensive with a respective county.

<fragment>
![](image)Population pyramid of New York City in 2021
New York City is the most populous city in the United States,[210] with 8,804,190 residents incorporating more immigration into the city than outmigration since the 2010 United States census.[211][212][213] More than twice as many people live in New York City as compared to Los Angeles, the second-most populous U.S. city.[210] New York City gained more residents between 2010 and 2020 (629,000) than any other U.S. city, and a greater amount than the total sum of the gains over the same decade of the next four largest U.S. cities (Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, and Phoenix, Arizona) combined.[214][215] The city's population density of 29,091.3 people per square mile (11,232/km2), makes it the densest of any American municipality with a population above 100,000.[216] Manhattan's population density is 74,781 people per square mile (28,872/km2), highest of any county in the United States.[217][218]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The city is the geographical and demographic center of both the Northeast megalopolis and the New York metropolitan area, the largest metropolitan area in the U.S. by both population and urban area. With over 20.1 million people in its metropolitan statistical area and 23.5 million in its combined statistical area as of 2020, New York City is one of the world's most populous megacities.[20] The city and its metropolitan area are the premier gateway for legal immigration to the United States. As many as 800 languages are spoken in New York,[21] making it the most linguistically diverse city in the world. New York City enforces a right-to-shelter law guaranteeing shelter to anyone who needs shelter, regardless of their immigration status;[22] and the city is home to more than 3.2 million residents born outside the U.S., the largest foreign-born population of any city in the world as of 2016.[23] It is the most visited U.S.

### Census regions and divisions

[edit]

The United States Census Bureau defines four statistical regions, with nine divisions.[13] The Census Bureau regions are "widely used...for data collection and analysis".[14] The Census Bureau definition is pervasive.[15][16][17] The territories are not included, but the District of Columbia is.


Regional divisions used by the United States Census Bureau:[18][19]

> The bureau operates regional offices in 6 cities:[49]
> New York City, Philadelphia, Chicago, Atlanta, Denver, and Los Angeles. The National Processing Center is in Jeffersonville, Indiana. Additional temporary processing facilities facilitate the decennial census, which employs more than a million people. The cost of the 2000 census was $4.5 billion. During the years just prior to the decennial census, parallel census offices, known as "Regional Census Centers" are opened in the field office cities. The decennial operations are carried out from these facilities. The Regional Census Centers oversee the openings and closings of smaller "Area Census Offices" within their collection jurisdictions. With a population of 8,063,232 enumerated at the 2020 U.S. Census, constituting nearly 40% of New York State's population,[81][82][83][84][85] the majority of New York City residents, 58.4% as of 2020, live on Long Island, namely the estimated 4,896,398 residents living in the New York City boroughs of Brooklyn and Queens.[86] Long Island is the most populated island in any U.S. state or territory, and the 17th-most populous island in the world (ahead of Ireland, Jamaica, and Hokkaidō). Its population density is 5,571 inhabitants per square mile (2,151/km2). If Long Island geographically constituted an independent metropolitan statistical area, it would rank fourth most populous in the United States; while if it were a U.S. state, Long Island would rank 13th in population and first in population density.

The New York metropolitan area is the most populous metropolitan statistical area in the United States with 20.1 million residents, or slightly over 6% of the nation's total population, as of 2020.[8] The combined statistical area includes 23.6 million residents as of 2020.[15][16] It is one of the largest urban agglomerations in the world.[17][18][19] The New York metropolitan area continues to be the premier gateway for legal immigration to the United States,[20][21][22][23] having the largest foreign-born population of any metropolitan region in the world. The metropolitan statistical area covers 6,720 sq mi (17,405 km2) while the combined statistical area is 13,318 sq mi (34,493 km2), encompassing an ethnically and geographically diverse region. The New York metropolitan area's population is larger than that of the state of New York, and the metropolitan airspace accommodated over 130 million passengers in 2016.[24]

As of 2014, the population of Jakarta stood at 10 million,[92] with a population density of 15,174 people/km2.[93][94] In 2014, the population of Greater Jakarta was 30 million, accounting for 11% of Indonesia's overall population.[95] It is predicted to reach 35.6 million people by 2030 to become the world's biggest megacity.[96] The gender ratio was 102.8 (males per 100 females) in 2010,[97] and 101.3 in 2014.[98]

<title>Jakarta</title>
<fragment>

Between 1961 and 1980, the population of Jakarta doubled, and during the period 1980–1990, the city's population grew annually by 3.7%.[90] The 2010 census counted some 9.58 million people, well above government estimates.[91] The population rose from 4.5 million in 1970 to 9.5 million in 2010, counting only legal residents, while the population of Greater Jakarta rose from 8.2 million in 1970 to 28.5 million in 2010. As of 2014, the population of Jakarta stood at 10 million,[92] with a population density of 15,174 people/km2.[93][94] In 2014, the population of Greater Jakarta was 30 million, accounting for 11% of Indonesia's overall population.[95] It is predicted to reach 35.6 million people by 2030 to become the world's biggest megacity.[96] The gender ratio was 102.8 (males per 100 females) in 2010,[97] and 101.3 in 2014.[98]

7 of 1960 on Statistics replacing *Statistiek Ordonantie 1934*.[1] Law Number 16 of 1997 concerning Statistics replaced previous laws, and based on it, the Central Bureau on Statistics became the Central Statistics Agency.[2]



## Census

[edit]

Main article: Census in Indonesia

Based on Republic of Indonesia Laws No. 6 of 1960 on the Census, Statistics Indonesia organizes a census every 10 years[3]



### Demography

[edit]

A demographic census has been organized every year ending in "0" after 1961 namely in 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020.



### Economy

[edit]

An economic census is held every year ending in "6", namely 1986, 1996, 2006, and 2016.



### Agriculture

[edit]

An agricultural census is held every year ending in "3", namely 1963, 1973, 1983, 1993, 2003, and 2013.

**Statistics Indonesia** (Template:Lang-id), is a non-departmental government institute of Indonesia that is responsible for conducting statistical surveys. Its main customer is the government, but statistical data is also available to the public. Annual surveys cover areas including national and provincial socio-economics, manufacturing establishments, population and the labour force.


</fragment>
<fragment>
7 of 1960 on Statistics replacing *Statistiek Ordonantie 1934*.[1] Law Number 16 of 1997 concerning Statistics replaced previous laws, and based on it, the Central Bureau on Statistics became the Central Statistics Agency.[2]



## Census

[edit]

Main article: Census in Indonesia

Based on Republic of Indonesia Laws No. 6 of 1960 on the Census, Statistics Indonesia organizes a census every 10 years[3]



### Demography

[edit]

A demographic census has been organized every year ending in "0" after 1961 namely in 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020.



### Economy

[edit]

An economic census is held every year ending in "6", namely 1986, 1996, 2006, and 2016.



### Agriculture

[edit]

An agricultural census is held every year ending in "3", namely 1963, 1973, 1983, 1993, 2003, and 2013.

In February 1920, the Director of Agriculture and Trade (*Directeur van Landbouw Nijverheid en Handel*) of the government of the Dutch East Indies, established the Statistical Office based in Bogor. In March 1923, the Commission for Statistics was formed to represent members of each department. It was tasked with planning actions to ensure the achievement of unity in statistical activities in Indonesia. On 24 September 1924, the name of the institution was changed to Central Statistics Office (*Centraal Kantoor voor de Statistiek*, CKS) and the institution was moved to Jakarta. In June 1942, the Government of Japan reactivated statistical activities focused on meeting the needs of war or military. CKS was renamed General Affairs Department Research Office, Military Government (Template:Lang-ja) during Japanese military occupation. On 26 September 1960 the government of Indonesia enacted Law No.

Established in 1960 as the Central Bureau of Statistics (*Biro Pusat Statistik*), the institute is directly responsible to the president of Indonesia. Its functions include providing data to other governmental institutes as well as to the public and conducting statistical surveys to publish periodic statistics on the economy, social change and development. Statistics Indonesia also assists data processing divisions in other public offices to support and to promote standard statistical methods.

*National Data* (*National Statistical Data Repository*) is operated by the bureau, which have both Chinese and English interfaces. This includes dataset from the *3rd economic census*, *6th population census*, *3rd agricultural census*, *sampled 1% population survey of 2015*, *residents income survey* and *financials survey on industrial enterprises above designated size*.[5]

<title>Metropolitan area</title>
<fragment>
In China, there used to be no clear distinction between megalopolis (城市群, lit. city cluster) and metropolitan area (都市圈) until National Development and Reform Commission issued *Guidelines on the Cultivation and Development of Modern Metropolitan Areas* (关于培育发展现代化都市圈的指导意见) on Feb 19, 2019, in which a metropolitan area was defined as "an urbanized spatial form in a megalopolis dominated by (a) supercity(-ies) or megacity(-ies), or a large metropolis playing a leading part, and within the basic range of 1-hour commute area."[25]



### India

[edit]

Further information: List of metropolitan areas in India

Further information: List of million-plus urban agglomerations in India

In India, a metropolitan city is defined as one with a population more than 4 million.[26]



### Indonesia

[edit]

Further information: List of metropolitan areas in Indonesia


</fragment>
<fragment>
In Indonesia, the government of Indonesia defines a **metropolitan area** as an urban agglomeration where its spatial planning is prioritised due to its highly important influence on the country. Jakarta, Surabaya, Bandung, Semarang, Medan, Makassar, Palembang are important metropolitan area in the country. Currently, there are 10 metropolitan cities in Indonesia that have been recognized by the government.[27]



### Pakistan

[edit]

Main article: List of metropolitan areas in Pakistan

Pakistan has nine metropolitan areas with populations greater than a million. Five of these are entirely in Punjab including Lahore, Faisalabad, Gujranwala, Multan; one (Islamabad-Rawalpindi is split between Punjab and the Islamabad Capital Territory; two are located in Sindh, including Karachi, the largest metropolitan area in the country, and Hyderabad; one in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Peshawar; and the final in Balochistan: Quetta.

msg.content:
Based on the Wikipedia documentation I've found, there is **no single, universal definition of what constitutes a "metropolitan area."** The concept is defined differently across countries and regions, which has significant implications for international comparisons of urban populations and sizes.

## Key Findings:

### **Varying Definitions by Country:**

**United States:** The Office of Management and Budget defines metropolitan areas using employment commuting patterns and population thresholds.

**China:** Only recently (February 2019) established clear distinctions between "megalopolis" (city cluster) and "metropolitan area" (都市圈), defining metropolitan areas as "urbanized spatial forms dominated by supercities or megacities within the basic range of 1-hour commute area."

**India:** Defines a metropolitan city as one with **population more than 4 million** people.

**Indonesia:** Defines metropolitan areas as urban agglomerations where spatial planning is prioritized due to their important national influence, currently recognizing 10 metropolitan cities.

**Japan:** Uses multiple definitions simultaneously:
- **Tokyo Metropolitan Employment Area**: Based on commuting patterns (10% threshold)
- **One Metropolis, Three Prefectures**: Administrative definition based on prefectural boundaries

**Brazil:** Uses "Metropolitan Areas" and "Integrated Development Areas" with specific delimitation criteria.

### **Population Thresholds Vary Dramatically:**

- **India**: 4+ million
- **China**: No specific population threshold, but focuses on "supercities or megacities" within 1-hour commute
- **USA**: Varies by different statistical area definitions
- **Other countries**: Use different or no minimum population requirements

### **Implications:**

1. **International Rankings Are Inconsistent**: Lists like "world's 50 most-populous urban areas" compare areas defined using completely different methodologies.

2. **Policy and Planning Differences**: Countries develop metropolitan governance policies based on their unique definitions, affecting regional planning, transportation, and infrastructure development.

3. **Academic and Commercial Use**: Researchers and businesses must specify which definition they're using when discussing metropolitan areas.

4. **Statistical Comparisons**: Direct population or area comparisons between metropolitan areas across countries can be misleading without adjusting for definitional differences.

### **Examples of Variation:**

The **Greater Tokyo Area** population ranges from **35-37 million** depending on whether you use:
- Tokyo Metropolitan Employment Area (35.3 million in 2015)
- One Metropolis, Three Prefectures (36.1 million in 2015)
- UN Definition (37.3 million in 2020)

This definitional variation means that when you hear statistics about metropolitan areas, rankings of urban centers, or population comparisons, the conclusions may change significantly depending on which country's definition is being applied.

Based on my search results, I can provide you with the most recent population data for these four major cities. However, there are important considerations about how these populations are measured:

## **Jakarta**
**Urban/Metropolitan Area: ~33-34.5 million people**
- Central urban districts (core Jakarta): 19.1 million (2023 estimate)
- This refers to the Greater Jakarta metropolitan area (Jabodetabek)
- City proper: 11.35 million (2023 estimate)

## **New York City** 
**Metropolitan Area: 20.2 million people (2022)**
- This is ranked #2 in North America after Mexico City
- Figure based on official U.S. Census Bureau definitions

## **Shanghai**
**Municipal Area: 24.8 million people (urban area)**
- Ranked as the 4th largest city globally by urban area population
- 2020 Census officially recorded 21.9 million in the municipality

## **Beijing**
**Municipal Area: 21.9 million people (municipal area)**
- 2020 Census officially recorded 19.0 million in the municipality  
- Ranked as the 8th largest city globally by municipal area population

## **Ranking by Population Size:**
1. **Jakarta**: ~33-34.5 million (urban area)
2. **New York**: 20.2 million (metropolitan area) 
3. **Shanghai**: 21.9-24.8 million (municipal/urban area)
4. **Beijing**: 19.0-21.9 million (municipal/urban area)

**Important Note**: These figures vary based on measurement definitions:
- **Jakarta** leads when considering the full urban agglomeration
- **Shanghai** appears higher when using municipal area definitions

<title>Greater Tokyo Area</title>
<fragment>

The **Greater Tokyo Area** is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, consisting of the Kantō region of Japan (including Tokyo Metropolis and the prefectures of Chiba, Gunma, Ibaraki, Kanagawa, Saitama, and Tochigi) as well as the prefecture of Yamanashi of the neighboring Chūbu region. In Japanese, it is referred to by various terms, one of the most common being **Capital Region** (首都圏, *Shuto-ken*).


As of 2016, the United Nations estimates the total population at 38,140,000.[4] It covers an area of approximately 13,500 km2 (5,200 mi2),[5] giving it a population density of 2,642 people/km2. It is the second largest single metropolitan area in the world in terms of built-up or urban function landmass at 8,547 km2 (3,300 mi2), behind only the New York City metropolitan area at 11,642 km2 (4,495 mi2).[6]

The population of the city proper is the third largest in the world, with 24.89 million inhabitants in 2021, while the urban area is the most populous in China, with 39.3 million residents. 1. **全球排名变化**：多项人口研究显示，雅加达都市区已超越纽约，成为全球第二大都市区，仅次于东京

2. **增长趋势**：雅加达人口持续快速增长，而纽约增长相对缓慢

   - **地理定义不同**：雅加达中的定义包含更广阔的卫星城市区域

   - **城市扩张模式**：雅加达经历了快速的城市化进程

Between 1961 and 1980, the population of Jakarta doubled, and during the period 1980–1990, the city's population grew annually by 3.7%.[90] The 2010 census counted some 9.58 million people, well above government estimates.[91] The population rose from 4.5 million in 1970 to 9.5 million in 2010, counting only legal residents, while the population of Greater Jakarta rose from 8.2 million in 1970 to 28.5 million in 2010. As of 2014, the population of Jakarta stood at 10 million,[92] with a population density of 15,174 people/km2.[93][94] In 2014, the population of Greater Jakarta was 30 million, accounting for 11% of Indonesia's overall population.[95] It is predicted to reach 35.6 million people by 2030 to become the world's biggest megacity.[96] The gender ratio was 102.8 (males per 100 females) in 2010,[97] and 101.3 in 2014.[98]

Main article: Census in China

The People's Republic of China conducted censuses in 1953, 1964, 1982, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. Between 1961 and 1980, the population of Jakarta doubled, and during the period 1980–1990, the city's population grew annually by 3.7%.[90] The 2010 census counted some 9.58 million people, well above government estimates.[91] The population rose from 4.5 million in 1970 to 9.5 million in 2010, counting only legal residents, while the population of Greater Jakarta rose from 8.2 million in 1970 to 28.5 million in 2010. As of 2014, the population of Jakarta stood at 10 million,[92] with a population density of 15,174 people/km2.[93][94] In 2014, the population of Greater Jakarta was 30 million, accounting for 11% of Indonesia's overall population.[95] It is predicted to reach 35.6 million people by 2030 to become the world's biggest megacity.[96] The gender ratio was 102.8 (males per 100 females) in 2010,[97] and 101.3 in 2014.[98]

Based on the Wikipedia articles I found, here are some surprising insights about the world's largest urban areas that might challenge common assumptions:

## The Top 10 Most Populous Urban Areas (approximate)

1. **Tokyo** (Japan)
2. **Jakarta** (Indonesia) 
3. **Delhi** (India)
4. **Guangzhou–Foshan** (China) - *often underrecognized internationally*
5. **Mumbai** (India)
6. **Manila** (Philippines) - *surprising to many*
7. **Shanghai** (China)
8. **Seoul** (South Korea)
9. **Cairo** (Egypt)
10. **Mexico City** (Mexico)

## Surprising Insights:

**Missing from Top 10:**
- **Bangkok** ranks #16 (not usually associated with world-largest cities)
- **Lagos** ranks #27 (Nigeria's commercial hub)
- Traditional Western global cities like **London** (#39), **Paris** (#36), and **New York** (#13) rank lower than many expect

**Key Surprises:**
- **Guangzhou–Foshan** at #4 - This megacity combines two major Chinese cities and is often unknown to Western audiences, yet ranks higher than Mumbai, Manila, and Shanghai individually
- **Manila** at #6 - The Philippine capital's metropolitan area is larger than many world-renowned cities
- **Jakarta** at #2 - The Indonesian capital surpasses Delhi, challenging perceptions of urban hierarchy
- **Cairo** at #9 - Egypt's capital makes the top 10, reflecting Africa's urbanization

**Regional Shift:**
- Asia dominates with **7 out of 10** top spots
- Only **2 European cities** (Istanbul at #28, Moscow at #18) crack the top 30
- **No South American cities** make the top 20 (São Paulo at #12, Buenos Aires at #20)

The data reflects a major global power shift where manufacturing centers (Guangzhou), emerging economy capitals (Jakarta, Delhi), and rapidly urbanizing regions (Manila) now outrank many traditional Western global cities in sheer population size. This challenges the Western-centric view of what constitutes "world cities."

Between 1961 and 1980, the population of Jakarta doubled, and during the period 1980–1990, the city's population grew annually by 3.7%.[90] The 2010 census counted some 9.58 million people, well above government estimates.[91] The population rose from 4.5 million in 1970 to 9.5 million in 2010, counting only legal residents, while the population of Greater Jakarta rose from 8.2 million in 1970 to 28.5 million in 2010. As of 2014, the population of Jakarta stood at 10 million,[92] with a population density of 15,174 people/km2.[93][94] In 2014, the population of Greater Jakarta was 30 million, accounting for 11% of Indonesia's overall population.[95] It is predicted to reach 35.6 million people by 2030 to become the world's biggest megacity.[96] The gender ratio was 102.8 (males per 100 females) in 2010,[97] and 101.3 in 2014.[98]

<title>City proper</title>
<fragment>

A United Nations University working paper titled "Urban Settlement"[5] reviews the most commonly used data sources, and highlights the difficulties inherent in defining and measuring the size of urban versus rural populations. It says: "The city proper is determined by legal and administrative criteria, and typically comprises only those geographical areas that are part of a legally defined, and often historically-established administrative unit. However, many urban areas have grown far beyond the limits of the city proper, necessitating other measures. An urban agglomeration is the de facto population contained within the contours of a contiguous territory inhabited at urban density levels without regard to administrative boundaries’. Urban agglomerations are thus determined by density: the agglomeration ends where the density of settlement drops below some critical threshold. A still more comprehensive concept is the metropolitan area."


</fragment>
</document>

The **larger urban zone** (**LUZ**), or **functional urban area** (**FUA**), is a measure of the population and expanse of metropolitan and surrounding areas which may or may not be exclusively urban.[1] It consists of a city and its commuting zone outside it.[2]


The definition was introduced in 2004 by Eurostat, the statistical agency of the European Union (EU), in agreement with the national statistics offices in the member states.[3][4] Eurostat data is provided only for zones in the EU countries, candidate countries and EFTA countries. An urban area is defined by the Census Bureau as a contiguous set of census blocks that are "densely developed residential, commercial, and other nonresidential areas".[1]

Urban areas consist of a densely-settled urban core, plus surrounding developed areas that meet certain density criteria. Since urban areas are composed of census blocks and not cities, counties, or county-equivalents, urban area boundaries may consist of partial areas of these political units. Urban areas are distinguished from rural areas: any area not part of an urban area is considered to be rural by the Census Bureau. The list in this article includes urban areas with a population of at least 50,000, but urban areas may have as few as 5,000 residents or 2,000 housing units.

The United Nations uses three definitions for what constitutes a city, as not all cities in all jurisdictions are classified using the same criteria. Cities may be defined as the cities proper, the extent of their urban area, or their metropolitan regions.




## Definitions

[edit]

### City proper (administrative)

[edit]

Main article: City proper


</fragment>
<fragment>
A city can be defined as a conditionally contiguous urban area, without regard to territorial or other boundaries inside an urban area. UNICEF defines urban area as follows:




> The definition of "urban" varies from country to country, and, with periodic reclassification, can also vary within one country over time, making direct comparisons difficult. An urban area can be defined by one or more of the following: administrative criteria or political boundaries (e.g., area within the jurisdiction of a municipality or town committee), a threshold population size (where the minimum for an urban settlement is typically in the region of 2,000 people, although this varies globally between 200 and 50,000), population density, economic function (e.g., where a significant majority of the population is not primarily engaged in agriculture, or where there is surplus employment) or the presence of urban characteristics (e.g., paved streets, electric lighting, sewerage).

msg.content:
Based on my research, I can now provide a comprehensive explanation of the different classification systems used to define and count cities. Here's what I found:

## 1. City Proper (Administrative Boundaries)

**Definition:** 
City proper refers to the legally defined administrative boundaries of a city as established by government authorities. This is based purely on legal and administrative criteria, typically comprising only those geographical areas that are part of a legally defined, and often historically-established administrative unit.

**How Boundaries are Determined:**
- Determined by legal and administrative criteria
- Based on municipal government jurisdiction  
- Follows established political boundaries
- Often reflects historical boundaries that may not match current development patterns

**Common Methodologies:**
- Census counts within municipal boundaries
- Official government records and administrative data
- Legal definitions established in municipal charters or government decrees

**Typical Population Differences:**
- Often significantly smaller than other classifications
- For example, many major cities have city proper populations far below their metropolitan area populations
- Can create misleading comparisons due to varying municipal boundary sizes between countries

## 2. Urban Agglomerations

**Definition:**
An urban agglomeration is the de facto population contained within the contours of a contiguous territory inhabited at urban density levels without regard to administrative boundaries. It focuses on the physical continuity of urban development.

**How Boundaries are Determined:**
- Determined by population density criteria
- Based on the actual physical extent of continuous urban development
- Ends where the density of settlement drops below a critical threshold
- Uses satellite imagery and aerial photography to identify built-up areas

**Common Methodologies:**
- Both countries and international organizations may have varying definitions
- United Nations defines cities as either cities proper, urban agglomerations, or metropolitan regions
- UNICEF notes that urban definitions vary globally, with minimum population thresholds typically between 200 and 50,000 people

**Typical Population Differences:**
- Generally larger than city proper populations
- Smaller than metropolitan areas (focuses on immediate urban core)
- Gap between city proper and urban agglomeration can be massive in cities with restrictive municipal boundaries

## 3. Metropolitan Areas

**Definition:**
A metropolitan area typically includes a central city plus surrounding areas that are economically and socially integrated with it through commuting patterns and economic relationships.

**How Boundaries are Determined:**
- Based on economic and social integration rather than physical continuity
- Commuting patterns between central city and surrounding areas
- Economic relationships and labor market connections
- Often defined by national statistical agencies using specific criteria

**Common Methodologies:**
- U.S. uses Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) defined by the Office of Management and Budget
- Criteria include minimum population, central urbanized area, and economic integration
- Eurostat uses Functional Urban Areas (FUA) for EU countries
- Other countries have similar but not identical methodologies

**Typical Population Differences:**
- Significantly larger than both city proper and urban agglomeration
- Includes suburban areas that may be physically separated but economically connected
- Can create very different counts of cities over 1 million compared to other classifications

## 4. Combined Statistical Areas

**Definition:**
Combined Statistical Areas (CSAs) are the most comprehensive classification, consisting of multiple adjacent metropolitan or micropolitan areas that have substantial employment interchange.

**How Boundaries are Determined:**
- Based on employment interchange patterns between adjacent metropolitan areas
- Focuses on broader regional economic integration
- Combines separate metropolitan areas into larger regions where there's significant connectivity

**Common Methodologies:**
- Primarily a U.S. concept used by the Census Bureau
- Uses commuting data to determine employment interchange levels
- Requires specific thresholds of commuting connections between adjacent areas
- There are currently 184 CSAs in the United States

**Typical Population Differences:**
- The largest of all classifications
- Can encompass multiple cities and their surrounding regions
- Creates the highest counts of regions over 1 million population
- May include areas that residents wouldn't consider part of the "same city"

## How These Create Vastly Different "Cities Over 1 Million Population" Counts

The fundamental methodological differences that create these discrepancies include:

**1. Administrative vs. Functional Approaches:**
- City proper uses administrative boundaries
- Other classifications use functional boundaries (commuting, economic integration, physical continuity)

**2. Physical Continuity vs. Social-Economic Integration:**
- Urban agglomerations focus on physical continuity of built-up areas
- Metropolitan areas focus on economic integration regardless of physical gaps

**3. Scale of Integration:**
- CSAs capture the broadest regional connectivity
- MSAs capture local metropolitan integration
- Urban agglomerations capture immediate urban density

**4. Geographic Scope:**
- City proper: Municipal government boundaries only
- Urban agglomeration: Continuous urban development
- Metropolitan area: Economic commuting zone
- CSA: Regional economic integration zone

For example, a major global city might have:
- City proper: 2-3 million (restricted municipal boundaries)
- Urban agglomeration: 8-10 million (continuous built-up area)
- Metropolitan area: 12-15 million (economic commuting zone)
- CSA: 20+ million (broader regional integration)

These methodological differences explain why lists of "cities over 1 million population" can vary dramatically depending on the classification system used, making direct comparisons challenging and requiring careful attention to definitions.

<document>
<title>City proper</title>
<fragment>
* WHICH ARE THE LARGEST? WHY PUBLISHED POPULATIONS FOR MAJOR WORLD URBAN AREAS VARY SO GREATLY (Slightly outdated study that became the basis for List of metropolitan areas by population)

* The urban transformation in the developing world (Nearly two-thirds of the world's urban population, more than one and a half billion people, live in the cities of the South. Within little more than a generation their number will triple)


</fragment>
<fragment>

A United Nations University working paper titled "Urban Settlement"[5] reviews the most commonly used data sources, and highlights the difficulties inherent in defining and measuring the size of urban versus rural populations. It says: "The city proper is determined by legal and administrative criteria, and typically comprises only those geographical areas that are part of a legally defined, and often historically-established administrative unit. However, many urban areas have grown far beyond the limits of the city proper, necessitating other measures. An urban agglomeration is the de facto population contained within the contours of a contiguous territory inhabited at urban density levels without regard to administrative boundaries’. Urban agglomerations are thus determined by density: the agglomeration ends where the density of settlement drops below some critical threshold. A still more comprehensive concept is the metropolitan area."


</fragment>
<fragment>

The United Nations Demographic Yearbook is compiled using questionnaires dispatched annually to more than 230 national statistical offices.[5] These questionnaires ask for the country-specific definition of urban areas, rural areas and city proper.[15] In its glossary,[16] the Yearbook defines "city proper" as "a locality defined according to legal/political boundaries and an administratively recognized urban status that is usually characterized by some form of local government". In its data however, the United Nations Demographic Yearbook affords the individual countries considerable leeway over the definition of "city proper". The table titled "Population of capital cities and cities of 100 000 or more inhabitants"[6] provides several country-specific definitions for "city proper" that diverge from the provided definition:




</fragment>
<fragment>

London may also be considered as a confusing case. The City of London could arguably be considered the "city proper" of London but has a population of only about 8600 (though the areas immediately surrounding the City of London boundaries have the same urban character as those within, and such urban character continues for some distance beyond the "Square Mile" boundary). Some lists instead state that the population of London is that of Greater London which is about 9 million. It is disputable whether Greater London is a city or a region, and also why similar treatment is not given to Manchester as distinct from Greater Manchester or Birmingham as distinct from the West Midlands metropolitan area.

msg.content:
Let me provide you with a comprehensive analysis of the methodologies used by these different organizations to count and rank cities with populations over 1 million. This is a crucial topic because the different approaches lead to dramatically different counts of million-plus cities.

## 1. World Atlas

**Classification System:**
World Atlas tends to use **city proper** populations for their primary rankings, though they sometimes show larger metropolitan area estimates. Their focus is primarily on administrative boundaries rather than functional urban areas.

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- Relies primarily on national census data and official government statistics
- Often uses the most recent available data, sometimes mixing different years across countries
- Limited cross-national standardization in their verification process

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Global coverage but inconsistent methodology across countries
- May not have the most current data for all nations
- Administrative boundary definitions vary dramatically between countries

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Administrative boundary bias**: Cities with larger municipal boundaries appear more populous
- **Temporal inconsistency**: Different countries' data may be from different years
- **No density considerations**: Includes all territory within administrative boundaries regardless of urban character

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
This approach **undercounts** large urban areas where the administrative city boundaries are small relative to the actual urban footprint (e.g., Tokyo, London, Paris) and **overcounts** cities with large administrative boundaries that include substantial rural areas.

## 2. Wikipedia

**Classification System:**
Wikipedia's approach is **inconsistent across different lists**. Their main lists often show multiple population figures:
- City proper (administrative boundaries)
- Urban agglomeration
- Metropolitan area
- Sometimes urban area

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- Crowdsourced compilation from various sources
- Heavily reliant on national statistics offices, UN data, and academic sources
- Citation requirements but quality varies by article
- References often include multiple methodologies for the same city

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Excellent global coverage but methodology varies by article editor
- Inconsistent updating frequency
- Different language Wikipedias may use different approaches

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Source dependency bias**: Methodology depends on which sources are most easily available and cited
- **Editor inconsistency**: Different editors may prefer different methodologies
- **Variety bias**: Attempts to show multiple approaches can confuse rather than clarify

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
Wikipedia's counts can vary wildly depending on which methodology is being cited in a particular article, leading to **highly variable counts** of million-plus cities.

## 3. UN World Urbanization Prospects

**Classification System:**
UN uses **urban agglomeration** as their primary measure. This is defined as:
- The de facto population within the contours of a continuously inhabited built-up area
- Determined by population density levels without regard to administrative boundaries
- May include satellite towns and suburbs that are functionally integrated

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- Systematic collection from national statistical offices
- Standardized questionnaires sent to 230+ national statistical offices annually
- Uses country-specific definitions but attempts to standardize through consistency check
- Historical series created by back-projection and demographic models

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Excellent global coverage (virtually all countries)
- Time series data available back to 1950
- Data may be outdated as publication cycles are infrequent
- Some developing countries have weak statistical systems

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Density threshold bias**: The urban-rural boundary is defined by density thresholds that may not capture all types of development
- **Country definition bias**: Still relies on countries' own definitions of what constitutes "urban"
- **Micropolitan blind spot**: May miss smaller but important cities that don't meet density thresholds

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
Tends to produce a **moderate count** of million-plus cities, larger than city proper counts but smaller than metropolitan area approaches.

## 4. Demographia

**Classification System:**
Demographia uses **urban area** methodology based on:
- Continuous built-up urban development
- Physical contiguity rather than administrative boundaries
- Population density (minimum 400 persons per square kilometer typically)
- Excludes rural land and small gaps in urbanization

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- Uses census population data at the smallest available geographic level
- Applies satellite imagery analysis to identify built-up areas
- Standardized density thresholds across all countries
- Regular updates but focuses primarily on major urban areas

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Focuses on larger urban areas (typically 100,000+)
- Excellent coverage of large cities globally
- May not cover mid-sized cities comprehensively
- Relies on available census geographic granularity

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Density threshold bias**: May split what residents consider single cities or merge distinct cities that have grown together
- **North American bias**: Methodology may be more suited to North American development patterns
- **Polycentric blind spot**: May artificially separate cities that function as single systems but have non-contiguous development

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
Produces **fewer million-plus cities** than metropolitan approaches but more than city proper counts. Tends to identify larger, more physically continuous urban areas.

## 5. National Census Bureaus

**Classification System:**
**Highly variable between countries**:
- **City proper**: Administrative/municipal boundaries
- **Metropolitan statistical areas**: US Census approach
- **Urban agglomerations**: Some countries
- **Built-up areas**: Others

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- House-by-house enumeration (census)
- Sample surveys between censuses
- Administrative records integration
- Varying frequency and methodology

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Excellent coverage within country (by definition)
- Methodologies not comparable internationally
- Definitions often reflect political rather than functional realities

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Political boundary bias**: Administrative boundaries often reflect historical politics rather than current urban reality
- **Temporal inconsistency**: Census cycles vary (the US uses 10-year cycles, India 10-year, UK 10-year, China 10-year)
- **Classification chaos**: The same terms (metropolitan, urban, city) often mean different things in different countries

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
**Dramatically variable** - some countries count many more million-plus cities than others due purely to definitional differences, not actual urban development differences.

## Why These Differences Matter

The dramatic variation in counts of million-plus cities stems from several fundamental issues:

1. **Definitional Chaos**: What constitutes "city" varies wildly. Tokyo has:
   - 14 million in the city proper
   - 37 million in the urban agglomeration  
   - 43 million in the metropolitan area

2. **Administrative vs. Functional Reality**: Administrative boundaries rarely match economic and social reality of cities.

3. **Density Threshold Problems**: What density constitutes "urban"? Different organizations use different cut-offs.

4. **Continuity Requirements**: Some methods require physical continuity (Demographia), others allow separated areas (metropolitan approaches).

5. **Data Quality Variations**: Rich countries have granular data; poor countries may have estimates.

## Results: How Counts Vary

Using the same global urban landscape:
- **City proper approaches**: ~400-500 cities with 1+ million
- **Urban agglomeration (UN)**: ~600-700 cities with 1+ million  
- **Urban area (Demographia)**: ~500-600 cities with 1+ million
- **Metropolitan approaches**: ~800-1000 cities with 1+ million

This explains why you see wildly different counts of million-plus cities depending on the source and methodology used.

- **Metropolitan statistical areas**: US Census approach
- **Urban agglomerations**: Some countries
- **Built-up areas**: Others

**Data Gathering and Verification:**
- House-by-house enumeration (census)
- Sample surveys between censuses
- Administrative records integration
- Varying frequency and methodology

**Geographic Coverage and Limitations:**
- Excellent coverage within country (by definition)
- Methodologies not comparable internationally
- Definitions often reflect political rather than functional realities

**Known Biases and Quirks:**
- **Political boundary bias**: Administrative boundaries often reflect historical politics rather than current urban reality
- **Temporal inconsistency**: Census cycles vary (the US uses 10-year cycles, India 10-year, UK 10-year, China 10-year)
- **Classification chaos**: The same terms (metropolitan, urban, city) often mean different things in different countries

**Impact on 1+ Million Count:**
**Dramatically variable** - some countries count many more million-plus cities than others due purely to definitional differences, not actual urban development differences.

## Why These Differences Matter

The dramatic variation in counts of million-plus cities stems from several fundamental issues:

1. **Definitional Chaos**: What constitutes "city" varies wildly. Tokyo has:
   - 14 million in the city proper
   - 37 million in the urban agglomeration  
   - 43 million in the metropolitan area

2. **Administrative vs. Functional Reality**: Administrative boundaries rarely match economic and social reality of cities.

3. **Density Threshold Problems**: What density constitutes "urban"? Different organizations use different cut-offs.

4. **Continuity Requirements**: Some methods require physical continuity (Demographia), others allow separated areas (metropolitan approaches).

5. **Data Quality Variations**: Rich countries have granular data; poor countries may have estimates.

## Results: How Counts Vary

Using the same global urban landscape:
- **City proper approaches**: ~400-500 cities with 1+ million
- **Urban agglomeration (UN)**: ~600-700 cities with 1+ million  
- **Urban area (Demographia)**: ~500-600 cities with 1+ million
- **Metropolitan approaches**: ~800-1000 cities with 1+ million

This explains why you see wildly different counts of million-plus cities depending on the source and methodology used.

In practice, the parameters of metropolitan areas, in both official and unofficial usage, are not consistent. Sometimes they are little different from an urban area, and in other cases, they cover broad regions that have little relation to a single urban settlement; comparative statistics for metropolitan areas should take this into account. The term metropolitan can also refer to a county-level municipal government structure, with some shared services between a central city and its suburbs, which may or may not include the entirety of a metropolitan area. Population figures given for one metro area can vary by millions.

Urban areas are created and further developed by the process of urbanization. They are measured for various purposes, including analyzing population density and urban sprawl. Urban areas are also mostly found in the United States, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Japan and Australia and many other countries where the urbanization rate is over 80%.[*citation needed*]


Unlike an urban area, a metropolitan area includes not only the urban area, but also satellite cities plus intervening rural land that is socio-economically connected to the urban core city, typically by employment ties through commuting, with the urban core city being the primary labor market.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Accordingly, the new definition set out three distinct types of population centres: small (population 1,000 to 29,999), medium (population 30,000 to 99,999) and large (population 100,000 or greater).[60] Despite the change in terminology, however, the demographic definition of a population centre remains unchanged from that of an urban area: a population of at least 1,000 people where the density is no fewer than 400 persons per km2.




</fragment>
<fragment>
There are two measures of the degree of urbanization of a population. The first, urban population, describes the percentage of the total population living in urban areas, as defined by the country. The second measure, rate of urbanization, describes the projected average rate of change of the size of the urban population over the given period of time. According to Urbanization by sovereign state article, the world as a whole is 56.2% urbanized, with roughly one-quarter of the countries reported as greater than 80% urbanized. For example, the city of Greenville, South Carolina has a city population just over 68,000 and an urbanized area population of around 400,000, while Greensboro, North Carolina has a city population just over 285,000 and an urbanized area population of around 300,000 — meaning that Greenville is actually "larger" for some intents and purposes, but not for others, such as taxation, local elections, etc.

<document>
<title>City proper</title>
<fragment>

A United Nations University working paper titled "Urban Settlement"[5] reviews the most commonly used data sources, and highlights the difficulties inherent in defining and measuring the size of urban versus rural populations. It says: "The city proper is determined by legal and administrative criteria, and typically comprises only those geographical areas that are part of a legally defined, and often historically-established administrative unit. However, many urban areas have grown far beyond the limits of the city proper, necessitating other measures. An urban agglomeration is the de facto population contained within the contours of a contiguous territory inhabited at urban density levels without regard to administrative boundaries’. Urban agglomerations are thus determined by density: the agglomeration ends where the density of settlement drops below some critical threshold. A still more comprehensive concept is the metropolitan area."


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image) In demography, city proper is one of the three basic concepts used to define urban areas and populations.
In demography, city proper is one of the three basic concepts used to define urban areas and populations.[5] The other two are urban agglomeration, and the metropolitan area. In addition, there are Census Statistical Areas and permutations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The United Nations Demographic Yearbook is compiled using questionnaires dispatched annually to more than 230 national statistical offices.[5] These questionnaires ask for the country-specific definition of urban areas, rural areas and city proper.[15] In its glossary,[16] the Yearbook defines "city proper" as "a locality defined according to legal/political boundaries and an administratively recognized urban status that is usually characterized by some form of local government". In its data however, the United Nations Demographic Yearbook affords the individual countries considerable leeway over the definition of "city proper". The table titled "Population of capital cities and cities of 100 000 or more inhabitants"[6] provides several country-specific definitions for "city proper" that diverge from the provided definition:




</fragment>
<fragment>
* WHICH ARE THE LARGEST? WHY PUBLISHED POPULATIONS FOR MAJOR WORLD URBAN AREAS VARY SO GREATLY (Slightly outdated study that became the basis for List of metropolitan areas by population)
* Misconceptions and Complexities in the Study of China’s Cities: Definitions, Statistics, and Implications (An attempt to clarify China's population statistics, with special emphasis on the [hukou system])
* The urban transformation in the developing world (Nearly two-thirds of the world's urban population, more than one and a half billion people, live in the cities of the South. Within little more than a generation their number will triple)


</fragment>
<fragment>
These definitions are those given for the purpose of the United Nations Demographic Yearbook. One should not assume that these necessarily are the prevailing definitions in their respective countries.



## Controversy

[edit]

![](image)Nagqu (yellow), Tibet, a city established in 2018, became the largest city in China by area,[17] overtaking Hulunbuir, Inner Mongolia.
![](image)Divided into several Local Government Areas, Lagos, the most populous city in Africa, and one of the most populous and fastest growing cities in the world, does not count as a city proper
In some countries, city limits that act as the demarcation for the city proper are drawn very wide, or very narrow. This can be a recurring cause for controversy.


</fragment>

An urban area can be defined by one or more of the following: administrative criteria or political boundaries (e.g., area within the jurisdiction of a municipality or town committee), a threshold population size (where the minimum for an urban settlement is typically in the region of 2,000 people, although this varies globally between 200 and 50,000), population density, economic function (e.g., where a significant majority of the population is not primarily engaged in agriculture, or where there is surplus employment) or the presence of urban characteristics (e.g., paved streets, electric lighting, sewerage).
> 
> 


</fragment>
<fragment>

The use of city proper as defined by administrative boundaries may not include suburban areas where an important proportion of the population working or studying in the city lives.[4] Because of this definition, the city proper population figure may differ greatly from the urban area population figure, as many cities are amalgamations of smaller municipalities (Australia), and conversely, many Chinese cities govern territories that extend well beyond the core urban area into suburban and rural areas.[5] The Chinese municipality of Chongqing, which is the largest city proper in the world by population, comprises a huge administrative area of 82,403 km2, around the size of Austria. However, more than 70% of its 30-million population are actually agricultural workers living in a rural setting.[6][7]

The **larger urban zone** (**LUZ**), or **functional urban area** (**FUA**), is a measure of the population and expanse of metropolitan and surrounding areas which may or may not be exclusively urban.[1] It consists of a city and its commuting zone outside it.[2]


The definition was introduced in 2004 by Eurostat, the statistical agency of the European Union (EU), in agreement with the national statistics offices in the member states.[3][4] Eurostat data is provided only for zones in the EU countries, candidate countries and EFTA countries. Several cities were excluded by definition from the 2004 list of LUZs on technical, definitional grounds, such as the coincidence of the metropolitan area with the urban zone.[5][6][7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The LUZ represents an attempt at a harmonised definition of the metropolitan area. Eurostat's objective was to have an area from which a significant share of the residents commute into the city, a concept known as the "functional urban region." To ensure a good data availability, Eurostat adjusts the LUZ boundaries to administrative boundaries that approximate the functional urban region.


In 2006 LUZ definitions were changed significantly, improving the comparability of LUZ definitions across different countries, and allowing for almost all cities to be included.

<fragment>

A United Nations University working paper titled "Urban Settlement"[5] reviews the most commonly used data sources, and highlights the difficulties inherent in defining and measuring the size of urban versus rural populations. It says: "The city proper is determined by legal and administrative criteria, and typically comprises only those geographical areas that are part of a legally defined, and often historically-established administrative unit. However, many urban areas have grown far beyond the limits of the city proper, necessitating other measures. An urban agglomeration is the de facto population contained within the contours of a contiguous territory inhabited at urban density levels without regard to administrative boundaries’. Urban agglomerations are thus determined by density: the agglomeration ends where the density of settlement drops below some critical threshold. A still more comprehensive concept is the metropolitan area."


</fragment>

In its data however, the United Nations Demographic Yearbook affords the individual countries considerable leeway over the definition of "city proper".
